case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
case.limits: The server test is a Ninth Circuit rule and has been rejected elsewhere. It also addresses display rather than the reproduction that training involves.
case.holding: Image search thumbnails were fair use, and the court adopted a server test under which a site that merely frames an image hosted elsewhere does not display it for copyright purposes.

case.why_ai_cites_it: It extends Arriba Soft to a commercial search product and supplies the argument that a system pointing at content is doing something different from a system republishing it.

reading.body:
The most useful thing this 2007 decision supplies to AI copyright defendants is a doctrinal wedge between pointing at content and republishing it, a distinction that maps imperfectly but suggestively onto the difference between indexing training data and copying it.

The Ninth Circuit held that image search thumbnails were fair use and adopted the server test, under which a site that frames an image hosted on another server does not "display" it within the meaning of copyright law. The court extended an earlier ruling to a commercial product, Amazon's search service, which matters because AI defendants arguing fair use face the same commercial-use hurdle. The case appears cited in 79 live AI lawsuits, across claims involving the display right, transformative use, and secondary liability.

The data identifies two limits that constrain how far the holding travels. The server test is a Ninth Circuit rule and has not been adopted universally, so defendants outside that circuit cannot rely on it freely. More fundamentally, the case addresses the display right, not the reproduction right, and AI model training centrally involves copying, not merely framing. The analogy a defendant draws from Perfect 10 must therefore bridge a gap the decision itself does not close.
